# The Mathematics of Portfolio Return (continued)

## Composite Returns {#a}

One of the ways asset managers demonstrate their competency to manage a particular asset class is to group together the past performance of a number of similar portfolios and sub-portfolios and calculate an average or composite return. Composite returns are typically calculated using one of the following three methods:

1. Beginning weight
2. Beginning weight plus weighted cash flows
3. Aggregate

The beginning market weight method is the simplest approach because it requires the fewest calculations. The drawback of this method is that the weights of the individual portfolios do not take into account external cash flows throughout the period, which can be significant. Portfolios that experience cash inflows during the period will be underweighted in the composite return, and portfolios that experience cash outflows will be overweighted. This issue can be addressed to some extent by applying beginning weights plus weighted cash flows (in effect the denominator of the modified Dietz method) at the expense of a few more calculations. The third approach, the aggregate method, combines all the portfolios into one "super portfolio" and in effect treats the portfolio as one single portfolio in terms of return calculation.

Sample composite returns are calculated in Exhibit 3.58 for the composite data in Table 3.15. The standard return methodology for the portfolios in the composite are modified Dietz (end of day cash flow assumption) with a 10% large cash flow limit.

> **Note**
>
> Of course, these methodologies may generate different results, but there is no structural bias, and each method is equally valid. Because of simplicity and ease of calculation the beginning weight method is my preference.

**Table 3.15 — Composite data**

| Portfolio | Market value 30 June (£m) | Cash flow 5 July (£m) | Cash flow 9 July (£m) | Cash flow 14 July (£m) | Market value 31 July (£m) | Return |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 15.7 | | | | 17.1 | 8.92% |
| B | 29.8 | | | | 32.3 | 8.39% |
| C | 41.7 | 3.8 | | | 48.7 | 7.13% |
| D | 57.0 | | −5.6 | | 57.1 | 10.75% |
| E | 205.2 | | | 49.9\* | 275.0 | 8.16% |
| Total | 349.4 | 3.8 | −5.6 | 49.9\* | 430.2 | |

\*Note that the cash flow in Portfolio E on 14 July is defined as a large cash flow for both portfolio E and in the context of the aggregated composite. Value of Portfolio E on 14 July is £208.7 million and the aggregated portfolio £350.2 million.

### Exhibit 3.58 — Composite returns {#b}

The return for portfolio E, taking into account the large cash flow greater than 10%, is:

$$
= \frac{208.7}{205.2} \times \frac{275}{(208.7 + 49.9)} - 1 = 8.16\%
$$

Using the beginning market value method, the composite return is:

$$
\frac{15.7}{349.4} \times 8.92\% + \frac{29.8}{349.4} \times 8.39\% + \frac{41.7}{349.4} \times 7.13\% + \frac{57.0}{349.4} \times 10.75\% + \frac{205.2}{349.4} \times 8.16\% = 8.51\%
$$

Using the beginning market value plus external cash flow method, the portfolio weight in the composite is:

**Portfolio A**

$$
15.7 + 0 = 15.7 \qquad \frac{15.7}{375.98} = 4.2\%
$$

**Portfolio B**

$$
29.8 + 0 = 29.8 \qquad \frac{29.8}{375.98} = 7.9\%
$$

**Portfolio C**

$$
41.7 + 3.8 \times \frac{26}{31} = 44.89 \qquad \frac{44.89}{375.98} = 11.9\%
$$

**Portfolio D**

$$
57.0 - 5.6 \times \frac{22}{31} = 53.03 \qquad \frac{53.03}{375.98} = 14.1\%
$$

**Portfolio E**

$$
205.2 + 49.9 \times \frac{17}{31} = 232.56 \qquad \frac{232.56}{375.98} = 61.9\%
$$

**Composite**

$$
349.4 + 3.8 \times \frac{26}{31} - 5.6 \times \frac{22}{31} + 49.9 \times \frac{17}{31} = 375.98
$$

Therefore, using the beginning market value plus external cash flow method the composite return is:

$$
8.92\% \times 4.2\% + 8.39\% \times 7.9\% + 7.13\% \times 11.9\% + 10.75\% \times 14.1\% + 8.16\% \times 61.9\% = 8.45\%
$$

Using the aggregate method, the composite return is:

First 14-day sub-period return using modified Dietz:

$$
\frac{350.2 - 3.8 + 5.6 - 349.4}{349.4 + 3.8 \times \dfrac{9}{14} - 5.6 \times \dfrac{5}{14}} = 0.74\%
$$

Second sub-period return:

$$
\frac{430.2}{350.2 + 49.9} - 1 = 7.52\%
$$

Aggregate method total return:

$$
(1 + 0.74\%) \times (1 + 7.52\%) - 1 = 8.32\%
$$

The large cash flow rule applies at the composite level as well as at the composite level. However, it is possible for the large cash flow rule to apply to multiple portfolios in the composite without triggering the rule at the composite level.
